source.title: Brane Supersymmetry Breaking and the Cosmological Constant: Open Problems

accepted.question_text: In non-BPS brane-world compactifications that try to absorb the brane vacuum energy into curvature of the transverse extra dimensions rather than four-dimensional spacetime, under what precise geometric and boundary-condition assumptions does a closed compactification manifold admit a global solution without reintroducing fine-tuning? In particular, when the brane tension changes because supersymmetry is broken on a codimension-2 brane, can the transverse geometry and warp factor adjust continuously enough to absorb that arbitrary tension, or do deficit-angle sum rules and other global constraints obstruct such solutions unless the model has at least two, and perhaps effectively codimension-3-or-higher, extra dimensions?

evidence.quote: The issue of boundary conditions: due to obstructions to finding a global solution for the background geometry, it has been argued [9] that the Rubakov-Shaposhnikov mechanism cannot be extended to models with a single extra dimension [10]. It will be argued that in order to avoid similar problems, at least two extra dimensions are needed.

As for the first problem, if we want to have a closed compactification manifold, we must actually impose boundary conditions on α(r) and g̃(r) both at r = ǫ and at large r. But there may be global obstructions to our ability to impose such boundary conditions.

Since only a discrete set of brane cosmological constants can be absorbed in the transverse curvature, there is no continuus "Rubakov–Shaposhnikov modulus" that can be adjusted to absorb this arbitrary brane tension.

accepted.question_text: Suppose a compact brane-world model has at least two extra dimensions and admits classical solutions in which the brane vacuum energy is redirected into transverse curvature. What dynamical mechanism then selects the phenomenologically required branch with four-dimensional cosmological constant k = 0? More specifically, is bulk supersymmetry by itself sufficient to make the k = 0 solution stable once supersymmetry breaking on the brane backreacts on the bulk, and once loop corrections generate an effective potential for the modulus k, or can that potential instead have its minimum at some nonzero value of k?

evidence.quote: The issue of nearby curved solutions: it remains an open question whether supersymmetry in the bulk is good enough to ensure that the solution where all of the brane vacuum energy is absorbed in the curvature transverse (rather than parallel) to the brane is the stable one.
But in this case we still have the second problem mentioned above. There are nearby curved solutions with k 6= 0. What picks the solution with k = 0?

Even if this potential is small due to the smallness of Newton’s constant, it is not clear that the potential is such that its minimum is at k = 0. Unfortunately this remains an open problem of the scenario outlined in section 1.

accepted.question_text: For concrete string compactifications containing stable non-BPS 3-branes, do the bulk supergravity fields actually acquire supersymmetry-breaking masses in the milli-electron-volt range predicted by volume suppression? Answering this requires solving for the eigenvalues of the scalar, fermion, gravitino, and related wave operators in the full gravitational background of the non-BPS soliton and determining whether the lowest bulk modes in realistic three-brane geometries, rather than only in toy models, scale as mbulk approximately mbrane squared divided by the Planck mass.

evidence.quote: It must be demonstrated in concrete examples that mbulk is really in the milli–eV range.
To actually compute the bulk masses precisely, one should find the eigenvalues of the various wave operators in the gravitational background of the non–BPS soliton

Generalizing the discussion to the three–brane geometry is left for the future; let us just note that it seems important to "get out of the throat", i.e. to not only restrict the discussion to the near–horizon limit AdS5 × S5.

accepted.question_text: Among candidate non-BPS soliton backgrounds that realize this brane-world scenario, which ones satisfy the consistency condition that the supertrace of the squared bulk supergravity mass matrix vanishes, Str M^2_bulk = 0, so that the induced four-dimensional curvature is not catastrophically too large? Since local supersymmetry does not guarantee this cancellation, the open problem is to compute the full bulk spectrum for each background and determine whether the required vanishing supertrace holds without fine-tuning.

evidence.quote: Even when this is the case, the bulk fields produce a curvature radius of the universe that is too big (of solar system scales), unless Str M2 bulk = 0 .
The question is then, is Str M2 bulk = 0 ?
So Str M2 bulk = 0 is an important consistency criterion that must be checked for each non–BPS soliton background individually.

accepted.question_text: Do the higher Kaluza-Klein excitations in these compactifications make substantial contributions to the four-dimensional cosmological constant through Str M^2_bulk or Str M^4_bulk, or is there a real mechanism that suppresses or cancels their effect? The scenario requires either that the Kaluza-Klein tower also obey Str M^2_bulk = 0 and contributes negligibly to Str M^4_bulk, for example because the mass splittings are tiny, or that some other unexpected feature of the effective four-dimensional Kaluza-Klein gauge theory removes these contributions.

evidence.quote: It must be assumed that Kaluza Klein modes do not contribute to the 4–dimensional cosmological constant, e.g. because their mass splittings might be very small.

What is a potentially fatal problem with our scenario, though, is the following. So far, we have only considered the contribution of the Kaluza–Klein zero modes to both Str M4 bulk and Str M2 bulk. But the higher Kaluza–Klein modes should also contribute.

We must assume that Str M2 bulk = 0 also for the Kaluza–Klein modes, and moreover, that they do not contribute to Str M4 bulk – either because their mass splittings are tiny, or because of some other unexpected feature of the effective four–dimensional Kaluza–Klein gauge theory.
